_readme: Public case-study content. Edit here, then run `node tools/build-case-studies.mjs` to inject it into case-studies.html as plain CS_DATA. This is the DECLASSIFIED version: no client metrics, no internal system names, no attributed failures. Same structure for every study so they stay scannable side by side: summary, meta (role/team/timeline/methods), an optional `pull` (a participant quote if `by` is set, otherwise a one-line takeaway), then the six fixed sections.

_template.title: One phrase, the headline
_template.summary: 2 to 3 sentences: what the project was and how it turned out.

pull.by: Attribution if it is a real quote, otherwise omit.

meta.team: e.g. 2 (researcher and designer) plus the client's product team

sections.body: The product, the team, why this mattered.
The decision the research had to inform.
Methods and scale, and what was hard about running it.
The findings, shown not just stated. Blank line between paragraphs.
What changed, what shipped, or the decision it drove.
One honest thing.

studies.title: Building a testing habit on the booking flow
studies.summary: Wizz Air's conversion team shipped changes to the booking flow quickly and mostly on instinct. Over about eighteen months embedded with them, I made research a normal part of that process rather than a step people remembered to skip.

pull.text: Once "does this need research" was a required field in planning, the answer stopped being silence.

meta.team: Part of a shared research function, sitting inside the Conversion Optimisation team

sections.body: The Conversion Optimisation team owned the funnel from search to payment and had aggressive targets, so it moved fast. Research existed as a shared service a few teams away, which in practice meant it got pulled in late, if at all, and usually to confirm a decision that had already been made. Design choices leaned on analytics and on whoever argued hardest in the room.
Two things. Which of the changes in the backlog actually help people book, and how do we stop the ones that quietly break the funnel from reaching production.

I worked from inside the team rather than taking tickets. Moderated usability sessions on flows that were still in Figma, so feedback arrived while it was cheap to act on. Preference testing when the team was split between two designs and going in circles, which turned an argument into a number. And a crowdsourced pass on real devices as the last gate before release, aimed at the browser and device combinations nobody checked by hand.

Alongside the studies I spent time on the plumbing, because one researcher cannot keep up with a team that ships weekly. I ran a short training so designers could moderate their own quick tests, put together a toolbox they could pull methods from, and got a field added to the planning tool that made a product manager state, in writing, whether a change needed research before it could move forward.

The pre-release testing kept catching things that had slipped through QA. The clearest was a change that blocked booking completely on Chrome for Android, a combination with real volume behind it, that would otherwise have gone live.

The preference tests were less dramatic and more useful over time. Teams had been choosing between designs with no user input at all, and were relieved to stop once it was quick to do.

The process change mattered more than any single study. Once the planning tool asked whether a change needed research, that question stopped being one people could quietly not answer.

Research went from something people asked for as a favour to a normal part of the process. The team started doing discovery and delivery side by side, testing happened earlier and more often, and the work fed into a rise in booking conversion over that period that the whole team owns, not any one function.

I leaned on being embedded and well liked to get the process changes through. That works until you leave. I would have spent more of that time getting one or two product managers to own the practice themselves, so it did not depend on me being in the standup.

studies.title: Shaping the topology view for Cisco Nexus Cloud
studies.summary: I was one of two researchers on the team that built the first version of Cisco Nexus Cloud. Most of my work was on the network topology view: whether a visual map of a data-centre network was actually useful to the people who run one, and whether we could make it usable. It shipped in Nexus Dashboard, and Cisco filed patents on the interaction model it produced.

pull.text: If I could show this to someone doing day-two support, I could sell it.

meta.team: With a product designer and a second researcher, inside Cisco's Cloud Networking design team

sections.body: Nexus Cloud is a tool for monitoring and managing company networks, especially across several data centres and cloud regions at once. The users are network administrators, cloud architects and similar specialists. They know their domain deeply and are quick to dismiss anything that seems to hide detail from them. I joined at the concept stage, working next to a product designer, with a second researcher on nearby features.
Does a visual topology view help these specialists work faster than the tables and command line they already use, and if it does, is the version we are designing usable enough to build on.

The subject matter is hard to get into from outside, so the research was mostly about testing ideas we already had rather than looking for new ones. Concept tests first, to check an idea was worth pursuing at all, then usability tests once a direction held. Every session opened with fifteen or twenty minutes on the person's actual work and what they were trying to get done, partly for context and partly because we could not assume we understood the domain.

Recruiting was the constant problem. The product was confidential and we had no route to real customers, so participants were internal Cisco network staff and a few partners who run large Cisco environments. We put the topology concept through several rounds, adjusting the prototype between each.

The visual view worked. People could see how parts of their infrastructure connected at a glance and move from a whole-network picture down to a single device without losing their place.

The feature they valued most was tracing a path between two endpoints across sites, which is a slow, fiddly job today when you know the two ends but not why they cannot talk to each other.

That same feature was the weak point. Almost every participant failed to find the mechanism for it and had to be pointed at it, so making it discoverable became the main thing to fix before rollout. Two smaller findings held up across rounds: people reached for search before anything else as a way into the topology, and signalling problems only through colour was going to fail anyone with a colour vision deficiency.

The topology work shipped in Cisco's Nexus Dashboard. The pin-and-trace interaction it produced was filed by Cisco as a US patent, granted in 2024, with a related one in 2025. I am not a named inventor on either. The product lead publicly credited the wider UX team, including me, as contributors to the concepts. My part was the research and the decisions about how the interaction should behave for the user, not the system underneath.

We did almost no upfront research into what users needed, because access was tight and the deadline was not. It meant the early concepts rested heavily on the technical product manager's read of the users, which was good but was one person's. A handful of contextual interviews up front would have given us our own footing to argue from.

studies.title: Making an AI recommendation tool one that account managers trust
studies.summary: Brenntag had built an internal tool that used machine learning to tell account managers which customers to call and what to sell them. The people it was built for did not use it. I spent about three years embedded with the team, first working out why, then using that to steer a full redesign and a change in how the predictions were presented.

pull.text: A prediction arrived with no reasoning attached, so the first time one looked wrong, people quietly stopped believing the rest.

meta.team: Embedded with engineers, data scientists and a designer on the product team

sections.body: The tool sat on a lot of order history and predicted, per customer, the risk of losing them, the right moment to prompt a reorder, and what else they might buy. The users were several hundred account managers across the US and Western Europe, most with six to ten years in the job and their own well-worn way of working. Take-up was low, and had been for a while.
Why do experienced account managers ignore the tool's recommendations, and what would it take for the tool to become part of how they plan their week rather than another tab they close.

A full cycle rather than one study. Stakeholder interviews first, including with the data scientists, so I understood what the models could and could not do and did not go on to promise things the data would not support. Then two rounds of interviews with account managers in the UK, the US and Poland, a survey on how they actually plan and prioritise their accounts, concept testing on the redesign as it took shape, and analytics plus a recurring satisfaction survey once it shipped.

The less visible part was showing up. I sat in every sprint ceremony, including backlog refinement, which researchers usually skip. It was the only reliable way to catch the moment a decision affecting users was being made and say something before it was made.

The tool was asking for trust it had not earned. A prediction arrived with no reasoning attached, so the first time one looked wrong, and some did, the user had no way to check it and quietly stopped believing the rest.

It was also making more work, not less. People still cross-checked every prediction against the reports they already trusted, and were entering much the same information twice, once into the tool and once into the CRM.

There was a mismatch between what the tool pushed and what the job rewards. It leaned on retention. Account managers are measured just as much on growth, so advice that only talked about churn felt beside the point. A churn risk shown as a bare percentage, with nothing behind it, got ignored.

The findings shaped the redesign. The interface moved to a three-level structure, so people could go from a portfolio view to a customer to a single product. Predictions were shown together with the data they were based on. A switch let people work in retention mode or growth mode depending on what they were doing. Each recommendation carried an estimated value over the next twelve months, so a busy person could triage.

Research went from absent to the place the team checked when a question about users came up. The work fed the team's sales-uplift targets over two years. I also helped set up a shared research repository so the insights did not live only in my head.

The trust problem was visible in the very first interviews, and for too long I treated it as something clearer explanations could fix. It took a while to accept that part of it was the models themselves being wrong often enough to matter, which is a harder and slower conversation with the data team. I would start that conversation earlier, with evidence in hand.

studies.title: Validating a new digital business for Bosch Power Tools
studies.summary: Bosch Power Tools had an idea for a digital business and no in-house way to test it. They also wanted their own team to come out of the project able to run that kind of test without us. Over seven weeks the concept changed shape, from a plain marketplace to something built around proof of quality, and we gave them a recommendation to build along with the main reason it might not work.

pull.text: Clients did not distrust tradespeople. They distrusted their own ability to tell a good one from a bad one.

meta.team: 2 (researcher and designer/lead) plus Bosch's Business Model Innovation team

sections.body: Bosch is a hardware company with limited digital-product capability in house. Through UX studio they asked us to test an idea for a platform that would match tradespeople with clients, aimed first at the Hungarian market. The brief had a second half that mattered as much as the first: their Business Model Innovation team wanted to learn this way of working, so the methods had to be ones they could repeat.

Is there a real unmet need on both sides of this marketplace, and if there is, is this particular concept strong enough to be worth building. I ran the work around the business model rather than the interface, because the decision was whether to build at all, not what the screens should look like.

Seven weeks. We started with a three-day workshop with Bosch's team, working through a business model canvas and a value proposition canvas so every assumption was written down and testable. Then about two weeks of interviews with clients and with tradespeople, some in our lab and some in the field at a tool supplier, because tradespeople are hard to reach any other way.

For the evaluation I started with a fake-door test: a real landing page for the value proposition with a sign-up to be notified at launch, and paid traffic to it. Sign-ups were close to zero, and the result was not even a clean no, because the traffic and the ask were both wrong. I stopped it after two weeks and moved to concept testing instead, walking people through a storyboard of the whole service with a clickable prototype at the point where they would have to commit.

Clients did not distrust tradespeople as a group. They distrusted their own ability to tell a good one from a bad one, so they fell back on people a friend or family member had already used.

Good tradespeople were not short of work. Their problem was standing out in a market full of poor operators, with no easy way for a client to see the difference.

Both sides had the same underlying gap, and it pointed at one answer. Built around a credible mark of quality rather than around matching, the platform would reassure the client and give a good tradesperson a way to stand out, in one move.

The research moved the concept from a matching marketplace to a model built on proof of quality, and we recommended building on that basis. We also named the main risk plainly: the whole thing depends on there being enough genuinely good tradespeople to populate it, and that supply looked thin. Bosch's team had done the fieldwork and the analysis alongside us and left able to run the same cycle on the next idea.

The fake-door test failed as much on framing as on traffic. "Notify me when it launches" does not fit the person with a burst pipe, or the tradesperson with a full week. If I ran it again I would look for intent where it actually shows up, which is in what people search for, not in a sign-up form.

studies.title: Where 3-D Secure breaks down at payment
studies.summary: New European rules added a bank verification step to card payments. Netflix wanted to know where in that step new subscribers were dropping out, and how much of it was Netflix's to fix. I led a three-month study that mapped the failure points and moved some of the fixes to the banks.

pull.text: The bank's screen appears in the middle of a Netflix flow looking nothing like Netflix, and people who were part-way to subscribing were suddenly not sure it was safe.

meta.team: 2 (researcher and designer) with Netflix's payments team

sections.body: 3-D Secure is the extra check, a code or an app confirmation from your bank, that European Strong Customer Authentication rules require during a card payment. It cuts fraud. It also puts a step between someone deciding to subscribe and actually subscribing, and any step there is a place to lose them. Netflix's payments team wanted to see that step the way a new subscriber sees it.
At which points in the 3-D Secure flow do new subscribers fall out, why, and which of those points can Netflix influence versus the ones that sit with the bank.

Two methods running together. A large survey across seven European markets to size where the problem was worst and get a first read on why. Then around forty moderated interviews where the person made a real payment on their own card, for a real Netflix subscription, and hit their own bank's real authentication screen. Not a prototype and not our mock of a bank page, their bank, so the hesitation and the confusion were genuine. We read the survey and the sessions side by side and compared how it played out market by market.

Failure was not spread evenly. It tracked how normal app-based smartphone banking was in a given market: higher where that was still new to a lot of people, lower where it was routine.

The weakest point was the bank's own screen. It appears in the middle of a Netflix flow looking nothing like Netflix, and often fairly plain, and people who were part-way to subscribing were suddenly unsure what they were looking at or whether it was safe.

The rest was practical. The code goes to a phone that is in another room. The banking app that is meant to confirm has never been set up. And the words on the screen, verify, authenticate, do not tell someone that this is the thing standing between them and their subscription going through.

Netflix used the findings to push for a cleaner handoff into the bank step and for wording that talks about the payment rather than about authentication. A good part of what we found sat inside the bank's screen rather than Netflix's, so the payments team took the evidence to the card issuers, to make the case that some of the checks were stricter than the actual risk called for.

Doing real payments with real cards was the right call and also a logistical headache that ate into the sample. If I did it again I would build the payment-testing setup and the participant screening first, as their own piece of work, rather than solving them study by study.

studies.title: A patient-first read on a clinical-trial platform
studies.summary: Medocity's platform runs clinical trials remotely, so patients take part from home. Years of added features had made it heavy for the two groups who live in it, the patients and the trial staff. A discovery project produced personas, a journey map, and an argument that the platform needed reworking rather than restyling. That argument didn't land, because the people paying for it couldn't agree on what the project actually was.

pull.text: For patients the trial sits on top of being unwell, and many do not feel unwell day to day.

meta.team: Solo through discovery, then with a designer

sections.body: Medocity is a US health-technology company. Its platform supports decentralised clinical trials, the model where a participant takes part from home instead of travelling to a research site. Two very different groups depend on it: the patients enrolled in a trial, and the investigators and coordinators who run it. Both had accumulated years of features and workarounds on top of the original product.
Where does the platform get in the way of what patients in a trial actually need, and is the fix a redesign or something lighter.

A six-week discovery, run solo at first and then with a designer. Interviews with patients who were in or had recently been in a trial, and separately with investigators and study coordinators. I worked the patient side up into three personas and a journey map that followed a trial from the patient's point of view rather than the platform's.

For patients, the trial sits on top of being unwell, and many do not feel unwell day to day. Against that, a steady stream of admin-heavy check-ins feels out of proportion. What people wanted was the platform telling them what was coming and what to do next, and some sense of not going through it alone, rather than more forms to fill in.

For the trial staff, running a study meant moving between four to six separate tools. Where a trial was partly in person and partly remote, they were doing the same work twice, once on paper at the site and once in the system afterwards. Smaller frictions stacked on top, down to 90-day password resets on a platform they have to be in every day.

The work produced the personas, the journey map, and a clear case that the platform needed reworking, not restyling. That case didn't land. The people funding it couldn't agree on whether this was a redesign or a facelift, the design lead left partway through, and the collaboration was paused, so none of it was taken forward.

I aligned closely with the stakeholders I worked with day to day and assumed that covered it. It did not. Before starting I would get everyone with a say over scope to agree, in writing, on what the project is and is not, so the findings have somewhere to go, rather than landing in the middle of an argument.
